Andrew Gilbert - Violin Prodigy

By: Julian Sun | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We profile 14-year old violin prodigy Andrew Gilbert

Summary:
Andrew Gilbert is a remarkable talent when it comes to playing the violin. At just 14 years of age, this St John's pupil has already achieved so much in such a short career. In this profile, we reveal the secrets to his success. Is it merely hard work or an innate musical talent that marks him out as special? We take you into the life of a normal South African boy with an extraordinary talent and the world at his feet.

Press Release:


Violin Prodigy
From the tender age of six, Andrew Gilbert has impressed with a distinctive talent for playing the violin. From joining the South African National Youth Orchestra at the age of 12, to touring with the Miyagi Orchestra and performing in the prestigious concert halls of Stockholm & Berlin. Carte Blanche meets a 14-year old with an extraordinary gift.


Script:


SCRIPT
VOICE OVER: The violin is a delicate musical instrument

And something that needs to be handled with care.

We’d all love to be able to play music but the cold truth is that whilst we might be able to strum a chord, the Vivaldi’s & Mozart’s of this world are few and far between.

Every now and then, somebody comes along who just takes your breath away…

Meet Andrew Gilbert, a 14-year-old boy from Johannesburg whose passion for music is exceeded only by his skill on the violin.

Since he was just 6 years old, Andrew’s impressed one and all. He’s a member of the Johannesburg Youth Orchestra & was accepted into the South African National Youth Orchestra when he was just 12. He’s also toured Europe with the Miyagi Orchestra that has seen him perform in the prestigious concert halls of Stockholm & Berlin.

Derek: Andrew I’ve looked at some of the videos, seen you performing on stage. What’s it like?

Andrew: It looks easy at first but it’s quite hard and it has to take a lot of dedication to do it

Derek: Well I tried; do you think I made a good start?

Andrew (laughing): No!

Derek: Why the violin?

Andrew: My mom would put on Classical FM and I heard an orchestral playing with violins and then I was like to my mom, “that’s the instrument I want to play. Please! I love it, it’s the best sound, it’s the best instrument to play!”

Andrew: “And then my God Mother comes to me with a violin case and I was so surprised, so overwhelmed, it was like the best day ever for me”








V/O: Music runs in the family and Andrew seems to have inherited his talent from his mother Yana who was once a concert pianist in the Ukraine.

Derek: Were you behind his God Mother giving him that violin?

Yana: No, no, my first thinking was to teach him piano. Both of my parents is classical musician, my mother is professional pianist, she is professor of piano and I’ve been brought up in musical family”

V/O: And at the age of just 12 he was already bringing the house down.

Peter: About 2 years ago when he was playing at the Linder Auditorium with Richard Cock. He received a standing ovation after the first movement, which in music terms, you have to wait till the end of however movements there are in the piece to applaud. He couldn’t bow because the piece wasn’t finished yet and people did not sit down and it was a packed house.

Andrew: I stood there and I was like, what must we do? Wait until they all stop clapping and then we started carrying on with the 2nd and 3rd movement. And then again at the end I received another standing ovation which was like incredible, it was like the best feeling ever
V/O: Andrew may have an innate musical talent but is his skill a result of nature or nurture? It’s a question that Educational Psychologist Ashley Jay is asked often

Ashley: In most cases it’s nature and nurture that contributes towards a child’s abilities. The support system is vital for any child but particularly a child that has the added pressure of um excelling in a particular area, who demonstrates exceptional abilities. They need more support.

V/O: Andrew’s talent would need careful nurturing. Enter Russian violin teacher Irene Tsoniff who’s been his mentor since he was just 6 and she demands hours of practice

Irene: You know, children really different and if child, catch him quickly and start to repeat after you immediately, you can see. So he was developing much, much quicker than other children the same age. Very, very musical.

Yana: When they young, they have to, you have to push them a little bit because they doesn’t know how to practice so I’ve been doing it since he was 6 and now obviously it’s become his habit.

Derek: So you do push him?

Yana: I do push him a little bit, yes.

Derek: A little bit?

Yana: Yes!


V/O: All those hours of hard work and practice have certainly paid off.

Derek: Andrew’s musical prowess saw him being awarded a full musical scholarship here at St John’s College in Johannesburg. And that’s where he came under the guidance of the director of music Ben Oosthuizen. Ben remembers the first time he heard Andrew play.

Ben: From the very first moment that he started to play, one could get the sense that there was something special about him as a performer. And within the first few bars I could easily sit back and relax and just enjoy his performance.

Derek: What struck you?

Ben: He played with great confidence and the fact that he also had an incredible ear, so the notes were played exactly in tune, there were no intonation problems whatsoever and extremely musical

Derek Here at St John’s, he lives the life of an average student as Andrew’s house master Daniel Pretorius explains

Daniel: Apart from being an excellent musician, he plays A-team hockey, he was the captain of our under 14-A soccer team last year. He plays cricket and he’s very good in the classroom too. So it’s wonderful to see boys making the most of the opportunities they get.

Derek: The stereotype is that classical musicians aren’t all that sporty but as you can see behind me, Andrew bucks that trend

Classmate 1: He was in my cricket team for my whole time at the Ridge School and we used to open the batting together. He was generally always selected Captain because he shows great leadership

Classmate 2: Andrew’s a very good sportsman. He played A-team sports I think throughout his time at the Ridge.

Classmate 1: I used to play piano and did drums. I gave them up because I just didn’t have the time. I find it hard to believe that Gilbert, who does the same work as me and he still finds the time to practice 2 to 3 hours a day. So I couldn’t do it, for sure.

Ashley: As far as practicing is concerned, if you tell me that a child is so psyched to practice, I don’t know, algebra, music, language, whatever they’re good at, I’ll tell you that you are lying.

Andrew: I usually come home about 8’o clock and I have to do my violin which is such a pity for me because I’m really tired but it’s also to improve my technical skills with it.

Ashley: I think it probably takes a hellava lot of motivation from his parents. It takes increased work ethic from him and I’m sure there are days where he just doesn’t feel like because at the end of the day he’s just 14.


V/O: It’s Tuesday night rehearsals for the Johannesburg Youth Orchestra. Andrew’s been a member of the JYO for the past 4 years. Conductor Eddie Clayton has watched his progress with keen interest

Eddie: He came in as a youngster, a tiny tot 11-year-old wonderful child prodigy with this amazing talent. And we immediately, we have this audition process and I immediately placed him in the first violins. He’s one of the most passionate young violinists I’ve seen in many years. The sound that he makes off the instrument is just amazing so his technique is fantastic, his intonation is good. He is an exceptionally talented young man. When you do identify that kind of talent, it’s a very rare thing and it has to be nurtured. And you run the risk of over-nurturing that and making it less enjoyable and thus killing that passion

V/O: But Andrew’s passion burns brightly. What will it take for him to fulfil his immense potential?

Irene: He can be professional violinist but for that he needs to practice more

Derek: He needs to practice more?

Irene: More, 3-4 hours that’s just to make up the programme which he’s playing. If you want to polish and like nail everything perfectly then it must be 6-7

Derek: That’s a lot of practice

Irene: It’s supposed to be

Derek: Doesn’t leave much time to play games

Irene: No games, no games for musicians, our game is the violin!

Eddie: The dangers of burnout in young kids is ever-present. My thinking very often is, you’re young once and you have these opportunities once in your life. He’s a very well balanced young man, amazingly.



V/O: Having shown such much promise, what does the future have in store for Andrew?

Peter: I’m proud with all his achievements. Obviously when he gets a standing ovation, the emotions are… you just can’t explain them. They are unreal and I had tears in my eyes to be honest. You’re just so proud to be the father of the person playing.

Yana: As a mother I’m very proud of him but obviously I would like to for him to achieve more.

Ashley: You don’t just need Andrew’s input, you eed his commitment, you need his buy-in. And if you don’t have that, it’s a no-go

Andrew: It takes about 20000 hours for you to be a professional violinist. I’m just maybe half way there, I still have a lot to learn.

Derek: So you’re not quite sure yet about whether this is the long road you want to take?
Andrew: Yes, I’m not quite sure yet. I’ll decide about Grade 10 or Grade 11 what I’m going to try and aim for

Ashley: This has to be a real family team effort because they have to look at what is best for Andrew, cognitively, emotionally, psychologically, occupationally

Irene: He can be professional musician in the future. He can make this a career. He’s got that talent and potentially he can but again, it’s his choice, to be or not to be.

V/O: Andrew’s future is still to be decided. Thankfully it’s not a decision that needs to be made any time soon. For now he plays violin for the sheer love of music. Whatever he decides to do, we will watch his progress with bated breath, after all, talent like this doesn’t come along every day and sometimes someone just comes along and takes your breath away.

Like Andrew Gilbert
